title: Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1915)
shortTitle: Bi-Metallic Investment Co. v. State Board of Equalization (1915)
summary: A generally applicable increase in Denver property valuations required no individual constitutional hearing.

sections.Parties: A Denver real-estate owner sued the Colorado State Board of Equalization, the Colorado Tax Commission, and Denver’s assessor to prevent implementation of a general valuation increase.
sections.Material Facts: The boards ordered a forty-percent increase in the valuation of all taxable property in Denver. The company argued that it had no opportunity to be heard before the increase. The Court assumed the same for other affected persons and city representatives. It also assumed that an owner with an unusually assessed parcel could use ordinary tax remedies for that individual disparity, so the challenged order concerned the common valuation principle.
sections.Procedural History: The Colorado Supreme Court sustained the order and directed dismissal of the suit. The United States Supreme Court reviewed the Fourteenth Amendment claim and affirmed that judgment in Justice Holmes’s opinion.
sections.Issue: Does due process give each affected owner an individual hearing before state officials adopt a general valuation adjustment applicable to all taxable property in a city?
sections.Holding: No. The Constitution did not require individual hearings before the across-the-board adjustment. The judgment sustaining the order was affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Holmes reasoned that government could not function if every broadly applicable policy required direct participation by each affected person. General laws routinely alter property interests substantially; political control over rulemakers supplies the ordinary form of protection in this setting. Londoner involved a small group exceptionally affected on individual grounds by allocation of a particular improvement’s cost. This order instead applied a common principle to the whole county’s assessments. The distinction concerns the nature and grounds of the decision as well as the number affected. Later assigned notes caution that numbers alone cannot classify every case, since legislatures can enact private bills and courts can hear class actions.
